source_span: Because Goldman's OECD commercial stocks counter remains resilient, the bank's $79 Brent fair value estimate is still $18 below market pricing, which embeds a risk premium for future draws and high disruption risk.
source_chain: Of the 543mb global visible stock draw since the war began, only 26mb came from OECD commercial storage (the category that actually prices Brent) — therefore OECD commercial stocks remain resilient — therefore Goldman's model fair value stays at $79, $18 below market pricing — therefore Goldman's forecast raise to $85/$80 for Dec 2026 is only 'modest' even though the bank now assumes Mideast shipping disruption runs into 2027 (helped by Gulf output returning to pre-war levels by 2H2027, 3.8mb/d new pipeline capacity, and China imports staying ~30% below last year). Invalidation: if OECD commercial stocks start drawing hard, or Gulf export adaptation stalls, or China resumes buying, the 'modest'/cheap-oil case breaks and price should run higher (Goldman's own upside scenario: Brent above $120 if 2027 Gulf output stays 4mb/d below pre-war).
pulse_chain: Brent's rise is framed as the market pricing disruption running into 2027, not a fading spike. The banks disagree on what that already contains: Goldman raised Brent/WTI forecasts by $5 to $85/$80 for Dec 2026 on the new 2027-disruption assumption but calls its own raise 'modest' — because of the 543mb/26mb OECD-commercial-storage split, which leaves fair value at $79, $18 under the market. Societe Generale, reading the same conflict, gets a $109 probability-weighted year-end price ($99 spot) with 30% odds a stalemate pushes Brent to $120 in November. Close: 'If OECD commercial stocks start draining fast, the cheap-oil case is dead. If Gulf exports keep adapting and China stays out of the market, the premium bleeds out.'
why: The pulse reproduces Goldman's exact chain — OECD-commercial-stock resilience → $79 fair value / $18-under-market → 'modest' $85/$80 raise despite a 2027-disruption assumption — correctly attributed to Goldman, and closes on the same swing-factor invalidation (an OECD commercial stock draw) the note itself uses, with the Societe Generale figures ($109/$99, 30%/$120-in-November) also matching their source (15776) exactly.
